rationale: B wins because it found the sharper fourth story instead of repainting the first one. Its "Can you trust shopping advice from an AI that gets paid when you buy?" is a clean user-incentive angle with a different protagonist, beat, and proof burden; A's "Perplexity Says It's Sharing Revenue With Publishers. It Won't Say How Much." is mostly the publisher-fight angle wearing a darker jacket. A also takes a few sloppy liberties with the record; B has one bad invented word, but it mostly keeps its hands where the facts can see them.
gaps_in_A: "for the first time, an AI search product is inserting itself into the transaction" is an invented market claim. The update says Perplexity is launching in-app shopping; it does not prove category firstness.
"publishers and their legal teams will need to respond publicly" overstates the consequence. They may respond, but the update does not force a public legal reaction.
"publishers are already being cited in answers whether or not they join the program" is not established by the update. That turns a fair question into a factual claim.

"Perplexity Says It's Sharing Revenue With Publishers. It Won't Say How Much." duplicates the first publisher/legal-threat angle. Opacity is a reporting hook inside that story, not enough of a new angle by itself.
gaps_in_B: "after months of legal threats" invents duration. The update says Perplexity has faced criticism and legal threats; it does not say months.
"live criticism and legal threats" may be true, but the update only says Perplexity has faced them. Don't quietly upgrade historical context into current active conflict.
"which merchants and product categories are live at launch" is the right proof ask, but without any named merchant in the update the commerce angle needs that caveat kept loud.
The publisher angle still needs one enrolled publisher on record. B says that clearly, but without it this remains a defensive company announcement, not a fully pitchable story.
